group.passage: Children around the world sing “do, re, mi” long before they can read music. Few of them know that these simple sounds were taken from a Latin hymn about a thousand years ago, as part of one teacher’s effort to save singers time. In the eleventh century, church singers learned their chants mainly by ear. The written signs of the day showed only whether a melody rose or fell, not exactly how far it moved, so every new tune had to be heard again and again until it stayed in memory. Mastering all the chants needed for the church year could take many years. Guido of Arezzo, a monk who trained the cathedral singers in the Italian city of Arezzo, saw this as a terrible waste of effort. His answer had two parts. First, he placed notes on and between lines, so that a singer could see the exact pitch of each sound. Second, he gave the notes names. He chose a hymn to Saint John the Baptist whose first six lines each begin one step higher than the line before. The words of the hymn were already old, but the opening syllables of those lines, ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la, became labels for the six steps. A singer facing a new chant could now match each note to a tune he already knew by heart. The method worked so well that Pope John XIX asked Guido three times to come to Rome and show it. The delighted pope then refused to let him leave until he himself had sung a melody he had never heard before. The names have changed a little since then. In the 1600s, an Italian scholar suggested replacing ut with do, which is easier to sing because it ends in an open sound. A seventh name, si, was later added, probably from the first letters of Sancte Ioannes, the closing words of the hymn. In the 1800s, an English teacher proposed changing si so that no two names would begin with the same letter, which is why many people now sing ti. Still, the basic idea has lasted: students who sing a scale today are using Guido’s invention.

translation_zh.text:
世界各地的孩子早在會讀譜之前，就會唱「Do、Re、Mi」。但很少人知道，這些簡單的音是大約一千年前從一首拉丁聖歌裡取出來的，是一位老師為了替歌手節省時間所做的努力之一。

十一世紀時，教堂的歌手主要靠耳朵學聖歌。當時的書寫記號只看得出旋律是上升還是下降，看不出到底差了多少，所以每一首新曲子都得一聽再聽，直到記住為止。要學會整個教會年度需要的所有聖歌，可能得花上好幾年。在義大利城市阿雷佐訓練主教座堂歌手的修士圭多，認為這件事是極大的浪費。

他的辦法分成兩部分。第一，他把音符放在線上和線與線之間，讓歌手看得出每個音確切的音高。第二，他替音取了名字。他選了一首獻給施洗者聖約翰的聖歌，這首歌的前六行，每一行的開頭都比前一行高一個音。聖歌的歌詞早已存在，但那六行開頭的音節 ut、re、mi、fa、sol、la 成了這六個音階的名稱。從此，歌手遇到一首新的聖歌時，就能把每個音對應到一首自己早已背熟的曲子。

這個方法效果好到教宗若望十九世三度邀請圭多到羅馬示範。欣喜的教宗後來甚至不肯讓他離開，直到自己也唱出了一段從沒聽過的旋律。

從那時起，這些名稱只有一些小改變。十七世紀時，一位義大利學者建議把 ut 換成 do，因為 do 以開放的母音結尾，比較好唱。後來又加上第七個音名 si，很可能取自聖歌最後的字 Sancte Ioannes（聖約翰）的開頭字母。十九世紀時，一位英國老師提議改掉 si，讓任兩個音名的開頭字母都不相同，這就是許多人現在唱 ti 的原因。不過，基本的概念一直延續下來：今天唱音階的學生，用的仍是圭多的發明。
